I have started state the issues of all 49 problems in the community-collected Open Quantum Problems list for the formal-conjecture project -- see the discussion there. I started to formalize two questions (existence of absolutely maximally entangled states, and number of mutually unbiased bases).

The formalisations are quite long and my question is whether this is because i do things highly inefficiently, or whether this is expected. Furthermore, would it reduce the size of the formalization if i use some of the formalized functions in PhysLib (reduced density matrices, computation of bases, etc)? Any guidance would be much apprechiated.

I'm not an expert in this area, and can't speak to the quantum-info side of things and whether there is anything there which will help. But I would say that your proofs their do look longer then expected, and can likely be golfed to be made shorter. Part of this may be down to thinking how your lemmas could be broken down into smaller general results which could be widely applied.

Hi! I think you'll definitely find a lot of relevant stuff in github.com/Timeroot/Lean-QuantumInfo (which should in O(1) days be merged into PhysLib).

A few problems, like MUBs or SIC POVMs, are definitely pretty straightforward to state on their own, esp. if you state them just in terms of Zauner's Conjecture for instance.

But a good chunk of those will necessarily require some theory of CPTP maps or mixed states, and I think that the definitions in our repo would be very useful for that.

I don't expect that the formal-conjecture project will want to rely on PhysLib. And honestly, some of them may just be too involved to state in formal-conjectures without some other dependency. For instance, the f-routing problem might be quite long to state.
I would mention, generally I would avoid any mention of vectors / kets, and try to do everything in terms of mixed states wherever possible. It'll come out much cleaner. (MUB is an exception to this)

Thanks for your answers. Very interesting insights @Alex Meiburg -- i do agree that stating the conjectures is better done without relying on PhysLib, and stating them in a nice way could be done much more generally. Let's say without PhysLib, would there be any (more general) strategy that would help me writing such proofs shorter? I think AME states might be exception to your rule too, as the conjecture talks about pure states per se - would you agree?

Alex Meiburg said:

I would mention, generally I would avoid any mention of vectors / kets, and try to do everything in terms of mixed states wherever possible. It'll come out much cleaner. (MUB is an exception to this)

maybe a bit parallel to the topic but: you mean this because of the current implementations or generally? Because I'm thinking as we move towards more integration with physics in general, whether working with kets will ultimately be more pervasive
